en: The Sūtra on the Power of Knowledge of Faith and Understanding Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperially Appointed Court Honorary Official,
Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master Mingjiao, Dharma-Bhadra, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

“Bhikṣus! You should know that all dharmas of the power of faith and resolve are dharmas capable of realizing the principle of ultimate truth; these are the dharmas of the Tathāgata’s fearlessness, which only a Buddha can know.”
There may be a bhikṣu or a śrāvaka who speaks thus:
"Regarding this Dharma of the power of faith and understanding, I have realized it as it truly is; my diligence is not in vain, and I am free from all dust and defilement."
Furthermore, he said:
"I am able to preach well; I am skilled in taming; I shall expound the Dharma, for now is the very time; this is the most excellent."
"One should cause others to rely upon this suchness; one should train in it and practice it with diligence.
Furthermore, he said:
"One should know thus: such a Dharma is most honored and supreme, beyond compare."
"One should see thus, hear thus, perceive thus, and know thus.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should know that all those śrāvakas who speak in this way are speaking falsely; they do not see thus, they do not hear thus, they do not perceive thus, and they do not know thus."
"Why is this? This Dharma is the true reality of all Buddhas; it can only be understood by a Buddha and is not a teaching shared with the śrāvakas.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Those who resolve with faith in the Dharma refer to the Tathāgata’s five powers and ten powers. What are the five?
First, the power of faith;..."
Second, the power of diligence;
third, the power of mindfulness;
fourth, the power of meditative concentration;
Fifth is the power of wisdom.
One who possesses faith and understanding is endowed with these five powers.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, being fully possessed of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, is able to thoroughly understand the unsurpassed state of a Buddha; moreover, he utters the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly and skillfully turns the sublime wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
What are called the ten powers of the Tathāgata?
They are as follows: knowing, in accordance with reality, what is possible and what is impossible.
To know what is possible and what is impossible in accordance with reality is the first power of knowledge of the Tathāgata.

As for this power of wisdom, it is only when the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are fully endowed with the power of wisdom that they are able to realize the unsurpassed state of a Buddha, to roar the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, and to skillfully turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s power of wisdom knows, exactly as they are, the causes, conditions, karmic actions, and the resulting fruits and retributions of all phenomena across the past, present, and future.

Thus, having known the causes, conditions, karmic actions, and the resulting fruits and retributions of all phenomena across the past, present, and future exactly as they are, this constitutes the second power of wisdom of the Tathāgata.

As for this power of wisdom, it is only when the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are fully endowed with the power of wisdom that they are able to realize the unsurpassed state of a Buddha, to let out the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, and to skillfully turn the sublime wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata, regarding meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and samāpattis, as well as even afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering—all these he knows with complete purity according to reality."

In this way, the Tathāgata, having realized as it truly is that he is entirely purified regarding meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and samāpattis, up to and including afflictions, karma, and suffering—this is the third power of knowledge of the Tathāgata.

As for this power of wisdom, it is only when the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are fully endowed with the power of wisdom that they are able to realize the unsurpassed state of a Buddha, to let out the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, and to skillfully turn the sublime wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the various faculties and conducts of all sentient beings.
Thus, having known the various faculties and conducts of all sentient beings as they truly are, this constitutes the fourth power of knowledge of the Tathāgata."

As for this power of wisdom, only when the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are fully endowed with the power of wisdom can they realize the unsurpassed state of a Buddha, roar the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, and skillfully turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the various inclinations and understandings of all sentient beings.
Thus, having known the various inclinations and understandings of all sentient beings as they truly are, this is the fifth power of knowledge of the Tathāgata."

As for this power of wisdom: if the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are fully endowed with the power of wisdom, they are then able to realize the unsurpassed state of a Buddha, to let out the lion's roar amidst the great assembly, and to skillfully turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows all various realms and destinies as they truly are.
Thus, having known these various realms and destinies as they truly are, this constitutes the sixth power of knowledge of the Tathāgata."

As for this power of wisdom, it is only when the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are fully endowed with the power of wisdom that they are able to realize the unsurpassed state of a Buddha, to let out the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, and to skillfully turn the sublime wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the dispositions of inclination and desire of all sentient beings.
Thus, having known the dispositions of inclination and desire of all sentient beings as they truly are, this is the seventh power of knowledge of the Tathāgata."

As for this power of knowledge, it is only when the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are fully endowed with the power of knowledge that they can thoroughly understand the unsurpassed state of a Buddha, roar the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, and skillfully turn the sublime wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata recollects the infinite dharmas of past conduct, namely: one birth, ten births, a hundred births, a thousand births, and a hundred thousand births; even up to immeasurable and boundless kalpas of increase and decrease. Regarding all such numbers of births and kalpas, he is able to recollect the names and clans of all sentient beings, their food and drink, their suffering and pleasure, the length of their lifespans, whether they lived long or not, and how they died here to be born there, or died there to be born here—including such physical characteristics, karmic functions, and other immeasurable and boundless matters of the past."

In this way, the Tathāgata, having known as they truly are all such past matters—immeasurable and boundless, including the dharmas of his past conduct, namely: one birth, ten births, a hundred births, a thousand births, and a hundred thousand births; even up to immeasurable and boundless eons of increase and decrease; and regarding these numbers of births and eons, the names and clans of all sentient beings, their food and drink, their suffering and happiness, the length of their lifespans, whether they lived long, or died here to be born there, and died there to be born here; and likewise their physical forms, characteristics, and karmic functions—he is endowed with the eighth power of knowledge of a Tathāgata.

As for this power of wisdom: if the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are fully endowed with the power of wisdom, they are then able to realize the unsurpassed state of a Buddha, to let out the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, and to skillfully turn the sublime wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

"Furthermore, with the pure divine eye that surpasses the fleshly eye, the Tathāgata perceives all sentient beings in the world—those born or passing away, those beautiful or ugly, noble or lowly, high or base, and those in good or evil realms—as well as the karma they have performed. He sees even those sentient beings who possess unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind; who revile the noble ones; who hold wrong views; and who perform unwholesome deeds and practice unwholesome dharmas—all of which arise from false causes."
Due to these false causes and conditions, after their lives end, they fall into the evil realms and undergo the sufferings of hell.

Furthermore, when sentient beings perform the ten wholesome karmas through body, speech, and mind; do not slander the worthy and holy ones; give rise to right view; and cultivate various wholesome karmas and practice various wholesome dharmas—all of these arise from true causes.
By reason of this right view, after the end of his life, he will be reborn in the heavenly realms as a deva.
He knows all such phenomena exactly as they truly are.

In this way, the Tathāgata, with the pure divine eye that surpasses the fleshly eye, beholds all sentient beings in the world—their birth and death, their beauty and ugliness, their nobility and meanness, their high and low status, their rebirths in fortunate or miserable realms, and the karma they perform—even down to those sentient beings who possess various unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, who slander the noble ones, give rise to false views, and commit unwholesome deeds and practice unwholesome dharmas.
Due to the causes and conditions of such wrong views, after the end of their lives, they fall into the evil realms and undergo the sufferings of hell.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, through body, speech, and mind, practice the ten wholesome actions; they do not slander the worthy ones or the noble ones, give rise to right view, perform various wholesome deeds, and practice various wholesome dharmas.
By virtue of these causes and conditions of right view, after the end of his life, he is reborn in the heavenly realms as a deva.
This is the Tathāgata’s ninth power of knowledge.

As for this power of knowledge, if the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas possess this power of knowledge, they are then able to realize the unsurpassed state of a Buddha, roar the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, and skillfully turn the sublime wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*); he possesses the liberation of the outflow-free and the liberation through wisdom. By means of his own supernormal powers, he fully understands all phenomena, knowing as they truly are: 'Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence. Such matters as these, he knows in accordance with reality."

In this way, the Tathāgata has exhausted all taints, possesses the liberation of the taintless and the liberation through wisdom; by means of his own supernormal powers, he fully understands all phenomena, knowing as they truly are: "Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence. This is the tenth power of knowledge of the Tathāgata.

As for this power of knowledge, if the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas possess this power of knowledge, they are then able to realize the unsurpassed state of a Buddha, to let out the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, and to skillfully turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"This is the Tathāgata’s power regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*). If someone were to ask:

'Regarding what is possible and what is impossible, how does the Tathāgata possess the power of wisdom such that he sees, hears, perceives, and knows them all, even unto the attainment of perfect enlightenment? "
"To one who asks in this manner, you should answer truthfully.

Furthermore, regarding 'the power of knowledge of all sentient beings' own karma': how does the Tathāgata, by means of the power of knowledge of karma, see, hear, perceive, and know it all, even unto the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment?"
"If there should be one who asks, you should answer truthfully:

'Furthermore, regarding all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis—how is it that the Tathāgata, by means of the power of knowledge of meditative concentration, sees, hears, perceives, and knows them all, even unto the attainment of perfect enlightenment?'"
"If there should be one who asks, you should answer truthfully:

'Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings and their various faculties, what is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding faculties? How does the Tathāgata, by means of this power of knowledge regarding faculties, see, hear, perceive, and know them all, even unto the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment?'"
"If anyone should ask this, you should answer truthfully:

'Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings and their various powers of faith, understanding, and wisdom—how does the Tathāgata, by means of his power of faith, understanding, and wisdom, see, hear, perceive, and know them all, even unto the attainment of perfect enlightenment?'"
"If there should be one who asks, you should answer truthfully:

'Furthermore, regarding the power of knowledge of the various elements of all sentient beings—how does the Tathāgata, by means of this power of knowledge of the elements, see, hear, perceive, and know them all, even unto the attainment of perfect enlightenment?'"
"If there should be one who asks, you should answer truthfully:

'Furthermore, regarding the power of knowledge of the inclinations of all sentient beings—how does the Tathāgata, by means of this power of knowledge of inclinations, see, hear, perceive, and know them all, even unto the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment?'"
"If there should be one who asks, you should answer truthfully:

'Furthermore, regarding the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of recollection—how does the Tathāgata, by means of this power of the knowledge of recollection, see, hear, perceive, and know all things, even unto the attainment of perfect enlightenment?'"
“If there should be one who asks, you should answer truthfully:

‘Furthermore, regarding all phenomena such as the birth and death of sentient beings, how is it that the Tathāgata, by means of the power of knowledge of the divine eye, sees, hears, perceives, and knows them all, even unto the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment?’”
"If there should be one who asks, you should answer them truthfully.

Furthermore, regarding the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*): how is it that the Tathāgata, by means of this power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, sees, hears, perceives, and knows all things, even unto the attainment of perfect enlightenment?"
"If there should be anyone who asks, you must answer them truthfully.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:

"This power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (sthānāsthāna-jñānabala) is taught by me only for those who possess meditative concentration (samādhi), and it is not proclaimed for those who lack meditative concentration."
Furthermore, this power of knowledge regarding karma, I teach only to those who are in meditative equipoise, and do not proclaim it to those who are not in meditative equipoise.

Moreover, this power of knowledge regarding dhyāna, liberation, samādhi, and samāpatti, I teach only to those who are in meditative equipoise, and do not proclaim it to those who are not in meditative equipoise.

Furthermore, this power of knowing the various faculties of all sentient beings is taught by me only for those who possess meditative concentration (samādhi), and it is not proclaimed for those who lack meditative concentration.

Furthermore, this power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations and understandings of all sentient beings is taught by me only for those who possess meditative concentration, and it is not proclaimed for those who lack meditative concentration.

Furthermore, this power of knowledge regarding the various elements of all sentient beings is taught by me only for those who possess meditative concentration, and it is not proclaimed for those who lack meditative concentration.

Furthermore, this power of knowledge regarding the inclinations and desires of all sentient beings is taught by me only for those who possess meditative concentration, and is not proclaimed for those who lack meditative concentration.
Furthermore, this power of knowledge regarding past lives, I teach only to those who possess meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and do not proclaim it to those who lack meditative concentration.
Moreover, this power of knowledge regarding the divine eye, I teach only to those who possess meditative concentration, and do not proclaim it to those who lack meditative concentration.

"Furthermore, this power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñānabala) is taught by me only for those who possess meditative concentration (samādhi), and is not proclaimed for those who lack meditative concentration.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Those who possess meditative concentration are on the right path; those who lack meditative concentration are on a wrong path."
"Therefore, you all should know this.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, received it with faith and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Power of Wisdom in Understanding through Faith Spoken by the Buddha.
